overview: Early medieval Armorica became a meeting place of local communities and migrants from Britain. Broërec was a particular region around Vannes within this wider story, not another name for the whole peninsula. The imported Broërec outline is misplaced far to the northwest; it should not be used as a reliable border.

periods.title: Armorica and Breton settlement
periods.summary: Sixth-century texts distinguish Bretons and Romans in Armorica.

periods.title: The Vannes region
periods.summary: Broërec developed around Vannes and later belonged to the Carolingian frontier march.

periods.title: Later connections
periods.summary: Regional rulers and counties became part of larger Breton political structures; surviving books illuminate later cultural continuity.

items.text: Similarities among Breton, Welsh and Cornish place names and languages support migration from Britain in the late fifth and sixth centuries. Its scale is debated: newcomers could influence existing communities without every family arriving on a boat.

The council of Tours in 567 distinguished Romans and Bretons living in Armorica. That is unusually clear evidence in a period with few written records. The peninsula contained interacting communities rather than a single population with one simple origin story.

Broërec belonged to the country around Vannes, between the Ellé and Vilaine rivers. The name is associated with Waroc. Geography mattered: this southeastern Breton region faced different neighbours and political pressures from communities at the peninsula’s western tip.

Under Carolingian rule, Vannes, Rennes and Nantes formed parts of a frontier march. Broërec later entered the larger Breton political world. The county’s territory eventually passed into the ducal domain, while its bishopric and regional identity continued.

At Lenn Sec’h in Caudan, archaeologists uncovered a farm used during the sixth to ninth centuries. Its enclosure covered about 5,300 square metres, bounded by substantial ditches. These traces give us a household landscape beyond the better-known stories of rulers and saints.

Pits at the Caudan farm were used to dry grain before it went into underground storage. A large, deep silo also survived. Getting the harvest safely through the year required planning after the cutting and gathering were finished.

One medieval building at Caudan was constructed on ground-level timber sills. The surrounding ditches reached roughly two metres in width and depth. Most of the building itself has disappeared, but the excavated layout still reveals how the farm was organised.

At Landévennec, excavation found a small early oratory surrounded by a cemetery. The monastery’s beginnings belong around the turn of the fifth and sixth centuries. The traditional story of Guénolé and eleven disciples is a founding legend, while the buildings provide physical evidence.

By the ninth century, after the earlier map phases, Landévennec’s monks copied books and followed the Rule of Benedict. A religious community could also be a centre of learning and a substantial landholder. Copying a book meant sustained skilled work by hand.

The excavated ninth-century monastery included a church, living buildings and a courtyard edged by a covered gallery. A Viking raid in 913 interrupted its flourishing life. Its long history helps connect the small early foundation with the more elaborate institutions that followed.

sections.title: A small word for the stars

items.text: In Pierre-Yves Lambert’s reading, the Old Breton word “nimer” means “constellation”. It appears above a Latin star-name in Angers manuscript 477, folio 14b. This is the scholarly transcription of an attested word in Latin letters; another scholar interpreted it as “number”.

The relevant part of Angers 477 was written in 897 and contains many Breton notes beside Latin learning. Scholars identify Breton scribes but debate where they worked. The book therefore illustrates later Breton scholarship and its connections, rather than a securely located school in early Broërec.

ending.text: Armorica and Broërec did not vanish when these map intervals ended. Local political structures became part of wider Breton kingdoms and the duchy. The Vannes region retained a recognisable identity through those changes.
